newsitem.title: USA: U.S. pork leader uneasy about monitoring stance.
newsitem.headline: U.S. pork leader uneasy about monitoring stance.

text.p: The National Pork Producers Council is no longer monitoring animal rights groups, a situation that has one of the group's officials uncomfortable.
"We are not doing it at the present time," said Al Tank, the NPPC's executive director. "I'm uncomfortable with it."

The NPPC came under fire earlier this year when it was revealed that some of the funds it received from the Checkoff program from the National Pork Board had been used to hire a Washington consultant who in turn "monitored" pork industry activists, environmentalists and animal activists.
The NPPC has since paid back the money to the Pork Board.
Under the federal Pork Act, 45 cents of every $100 of pork sold in the U.S. goes to the Checkoff Fund which is supposed to be used exclusively for promotion, research and consumer education.

During a press conference at the World Pork Congress here, Tank said animal rights groups are very well organized and the pork industry needs to be aware of their activities to better defend against them.
"The animal rights community has been very aggressive about attacking the pork industry head on," he said.
"They are flanking us in any number of ways, in the USDA, in schools and other organizations. That's why we want to know what they are doing and who they are aligning themselves with," said Tank.
Tank said the National Pork Board and the NPPC are currently in talks with USDA to better define the parameters for which it can use Pork Checkoff money.
"That's why we are not doing anything," he said referring to monitoring of animal rights groups.
The mandatory pork check off has been in place for 10 yeas and the $58 million it raises annually is administered by the National Pork Board.
Carnell Korsmeyer, president of the National Pork Board, said during meetings with USDA the pork groups were told they cannot investigate animal rights organizations.
"We can monitor the issues, but we can't look into their organization," she said.
